resources.string: deleted and handed back to free space
These changed after the scan (or their app was reinstalled), so they were kept.
See how much cache every app is holding
Caches, thumbnails, abandoned temporary files and duplicate installers. Anything less certain waits for your review.
Every item is verified again at the moment of deletion — size, date and rule. Links are never followed outside a junk folder.
Photos, videos, music and documents are never judged by name. Nothing is uploaded; there\'s no internet access at all.
Cached files apps keep in shared storage

Each folder is an installed app\'s own \"cache\" folder. Android requires apps to cope with their cache disappearing at any time and to rebuild it when needed, so clearing it never loses settings, accounts or saved content — the app may just load a little slower the first time.
Preview images galleries rebuild on demand

\".thumbnails\" folders hold small preview copies of your photos and videos, made by gallery apps for faster browsing. Your originals aren\'t touched. Galleries regenerate the previews the next time they need them.
Abandoned temp files and unfinished downloads

Files with temporary or partial-download extensions (.tmp, .temp, .crdownload, .part, .partial) and saves Android itself marked as never finished. Only files untouched for at least the minimum age in Settings are offered, so nothing still being written is included.
Diagnostic logs, crash and heap dumps

Log files (.log), crash dumps (.dmp) and memory dumps (.hprof) written by apps for troubleshooting. They\'re never needed for an app to work. Files inside your own folders (Documents, Download, DCIM, Music and so on) are never included here.

Windows and macOS quietly add these index and metadata files when storage is connected to a computer. Android never reads them. \"._\" files are only included when they\'re small enough to be Finder metadata.
APKs for apps you already have

Each installer belongs to an app that\'s already installed at the same or a newer version, so the file is no longer needed. Removing it doesn\'t affect the installed app. Keep one only if you want to downgrade later.
APKs for apps that aren\'t installed
Installers for apps that aren\'t installed, are newer than what you have, or can\'t be read (often an incomplete download). You may be keeping some on purpose, so check the list before cleaning.

These folders are named after apps that are no longer installed on this device. They\'re usually useless, but some apps save photos, recordings or backups in their folder — items holding media are marked. If you plan to reinstall the app, keep its folder.
Files you deleted, kept for 30 days

Items you\'ve already moved to the trash in Photos or Files. Android keeps them for up to 30 days in case you change your mind, then deletes them itself. Cleaning them now frees the space immediately — but they can\'t be restored afterwards.

Device Housekeeping works entirely on your device. It reads file names, sizes and dates to find junk — never file contents — and keeps its cleaning log locally. There\'s no account, no analytics and no internet access.
What gets cleaned, and what doesn\'t
Why is there no RAM booster?
Android manages memory itself and reloads anything a \"booster\" closes, using more battery to do so. Free RAM is wasted RAM — so this app doesn\'t pretend otherwise.
Why can\'t it clear every app\'s cache with one tap?

Since Android 11 only the system may delete other apps\' caches. The App caches screen shows exactly how much each app holds and hands you Android\'s own one-step clear for shared-storage caches, plus a shortcut to each app\'s App info for the rest. Android also trims caches automatically when space runs low.

A Safe category is defined by a rule that leaves no doubt: an app\'s cache folder, a regenerable thumbnail cache, a temp or partial file untouched for a day, a log, PC metadata, or an installer for an app you already have. Only these are preselected.

Review items are very likely junk but could matter to you — a leftover folder an uninstalled app saved photos in, an installer you\'re keeping, or something in the recycle bin. They\'re never selected unless you choose them.

\"Freed\" adds up the sizes of the deleted files. \"Measured\" is the change in free space the file system reports, which also reflects block rounding and other apps writing at the same time. Both are shown so the gain is real, not estimated.
Why does it need All files access?
Junk is spread across shared storage, so a cleaner has to be able to list it. The app reads only names, sizes and dates, has no internet permission, and every deletion is shown to you first.
